translations.literal: Both sons were all gold-sable ministers and colonels, arrayed at the emperor’s side.
translations.idiomatic: Both sons wore the gold-sable insignia of senior ministers and stood beside the throne.

sentences.zh: 方之古人，責深負重，雖舉門盡死，猶不稱位。

translations.literal: Compared to men of antiquity, burden was deep and load was heavy; although the whole gate all died, still it would not match the position.
translations.idiomatic: Measured against ancient exemplars, his responsibilities were crushing: even if his entire house perished in service, it would scarcely repay such honors.

sentences.zh: 而乃驕奢過度，名被九域，行不履道，而享位非常。

translations.literal: Yet then arrogant extravagance exceeded measure; fame covered the nine regions; conduct did not tread the Way, yet he enjoyed position beyond the norm.
translations.idiomatic: Instead he flaunted luxury, his fame filled the nine provinces, his conduct strayed from the Way, yet he kept rank far above his deserts.

sentences.zh: 以古義言之，非惟失輔相之宜，違斷金之利也。

translations.literal: Speaking by ancient meaning, not only did he lose assistant minister’s propriety, he violated the profit of cleaving gold.
translations.idiomatic: By classical standards he failed not only the chancellor’s role but also the solidarity expected of high ministers.

sentences.zh: 穢皇代之美，壞人倫之教，生天下之醜，示後生之傲，莫大於此。

translations.literal: He defiled the imperial age’s beauty, ruined human relations’ teaching, gave birth to all under Heaven’s ugliness, showed later-born’s arrogance; nothing is greater than this.
translations.idiomatic: Nothing could stain our brilliant age more, corrupt public morals further, breed wider scandal, or teach the young such arrogance.

sentences.zh: 自近世以來，宰臣輔相，未有受垢辱之聲，被有司之劾，父子塵累而蒙恩貸若曾者也。

translations.literal: Since recent generations, chief ministers and assisting chancellors, there has not been one who received filthy shame’s reputation, bore relevant offices’ impeachment, father and son dust-heaped yet received grace and pardon like Zeng.
translations.idiomatic: Never in living memory has a chief minister kept such a reek of scandal, weathered impeachment, and still seen father and son pardoned together as He Zeng did.

sentences.zh: 周公吊二季之陵遲，哀大教之不行，於是作諡以紀其終。

translations.literal: The Duke of Zhou mourned the two seasons’ decline, pitied great teaching’s not being practiced; thereupon he made posthumous titles to record their ends.
translations.idiomatic: The Duke of Zhou mourned the twilight of the two Zhou lines and, grieving that the great teaching went unheeded, invented posthumous names to mark how men ended.

sentences.zh: 曾參奉之，啟手歸全，易簀而沒，蓋明慎終，死而後已。

translations.literal: Zeng Shen upheld it, opened hands returning whole, changed mat and died; thus clarifying careful end, dying and afterward stopping.
translations.idiomatic: Zeng Shen followed that lesson, straightening his limbs on his deathbed and refusing an improper mat—proof that a gentleman minds his end to the last breath.

sentences.zh: 齊之史氏，亂世陪臣耳，猶書君賊，累死不懲。

translations.literal: Qi’s scribe clan, in a chaotic age mere retainers, still wrote the lord as bandit; piled deaths were not punished.
translations.idiomatic: Even Qi’s petty scribes in a lawless age branded a murderous lord in their chronicles and never tired of punishing evil.

sentences.zh: 況於皇代守典之官，敢畏強盛，而不盡禮。

translations.literal: How much more for imperial-age officials who guard the canons—how dare they fear the powerful and strong and not exhaust ritual.
translations.idiomatic: How much less may officers of this sacred court, whose duty is the law, shrink from the mighty and shirk full observance of ritual.”

sentences.zh: 管子有言：「禮義廉恥，是謂四維，四維不張，國乃滅亡。

translations.literal: Guanzi had words: “Ritual, righteousness, integrity, and shame are called the four cords; if the four cords are not stretched, the state then perishes.”
translations.idiomatic: Guan Zhong said, “Propriety, justice, integrity, and honor are the four stays of the state; let them slacken and the realm falls.”

sentences.zh: 」宰相大臣，人之表儀，若生極其情，死又無貶，是則帝室無正刑也。

translations.literal: ” Chancellor great ministers are people’s model; if in life they exhaust their passions, in death again have no demotion, then this is that the imperial house lacks correct punishment.
translations.idiomatic: Chief ministers set the standard for all mankind: if they indulge every whim in life and escape censure in death, the throne has no just law left.”

sentences.zh: 王公貴人，復何畏哉！

translations.literal: Kings, dukes, and noble men—what again is there to fear!”
translations.idiomatic: What restraint would be left for kings and nobles?”

sentences.zh: 所謂四維，復何寄乎！

translations.literal: What is called the four cords—what again is there to rely on!”
translations.idiomatic: Where then could the four moral stays find any purchase?”

sentences.zh: 謹按《諡法》：「名與實爽曰繆，怙亂肆行曰醜。

translations.literal: Respectfully according to the Posthumous-title Law: “Name and substance diverging is called miu; relying on chaos and running wild is called chou.”
translations.idiomatic: The statutes on posthumous names read, “When name and deed disagree, call it *miu*; when a man clings to chaos and acts wantonly, call it *chou*.”

sentences.zh: 」曾之行己，皆與此同，宜諡繆醜公。

translations.literal: ” Zeng’s conduct in all matches this; he should be posthumously titled Miu-chou duke.”
translations.idiomatic: He Zeng’s life fits both definitions; let him be posthumously styled Duke of Falsehood and Shame.”

sentences.zh: 時雖不同秀議，而聞者懼焉。

translations.literal: At the time although they did not agree with Xiu’s deliberation, yet those who heard were fearful.
translations.idiomatic: The court rejected his proposal, yet everyone who heard it shivered.

sentences.zh: 秀性忌讒佞，疾之如仇，素輕鄙賈充，及伐吳之役，聞其為大都督，謂所親者曰：「充文案小才，乃居伐國大任，吾將哭以送師。

translations.literal: Xiu by nature hated slander and flattery, hated them like enemies, always despised Jia Chong; when it came to the campaign of attacking Wu, hearing that he was Grand Commander, he said to those close: “Chong is clerkly pattern small talent, yet occupies attacking a great state’s great charge; I will weep to send off the army.”
translations.idiomatic: Qin Xiu detested flatterers and despised Jia Chong. When he learned that Jia had been named grand commander against Wu, he told friends, “That man is a petty clerk, not the leader of a conqueror’s host—I mean to weep the armies on their way as Jian Shu wept for Qin.”

sentences.zh: 」或止秀曰：「昔蹇叔知秦軍必敗，故哭送其子耳。

translations.literal: ” Someone stopped Xiu, saying, “Formerly Jian Shu knew Qin’s army must be defeated, therefore wept sending off his son, that is all.”
translations.idiomatic: Friends urged him, “Jian Shu wept only because he foresaw disaster for his own son’s campaign.”

sentences.zh: 今吳君無道，國有自亡之形，群率踐境，將不戰而潰。

translations.literal: Now Wu’s lord lacks the Way; the state has a form of self-perishing; hosts of commanders tread its territory; they will without battle melt away.
translations.idiomatic: Wu’s tyrant has doomed his state; our hosts already cross his borders and will collapse him without a fight.”

sentences.zh: 子之哭也，既為不智，乃不赦之罪。

translations.literal: Your weeping is already unwise, and is an unpardonable crime.”
translations.idiomatic: Your mourning would be folly and a capital offense.”

sentences.zh: 」於是乃止。

translations.literal: ” Thereupon he stopped.
translations.idiomatic: He gave up the idea.

sentences.zh: 及孫皓降于王濬，充未之知，方以吳未可平，抗表請班師。

translations.literal: When Sun Hao surrendered to Wang Jun, Chong did not yet know it, was just holding that Wu could not yet be pacified, submitted a memorial resisting requesting to withdraw the army.
translations.idiomatic: When Sun Hao had already surrendered to Wang Jun, Jia Chong still thought Wu unbeaten and memorialized to recall the army.

sentences.zh: 充表與告捷同至，朝野以充位居人上，智出人下，僉以秀為知言。

translations.literal: Chong’s memorial and the victory report arrived together; court and countryside because Chong’s position was above people, wisdom below people, all held Xiu as knowing speech.
translations.idiomatic: His recall petition arrived with the victory dispatch, and everyone agreed that Jia Chong outranked all men in office but fell below them in sense—proof that Qin Xiu had spoken true.

sentences.zh: 及充薨，秀議曰：「充舍宗族弗授，而以異姓為後，悖禮溺情，以亂大倫。

translations.literal: When Chong died, Xiu deliberated, saying: “Chong cast aside the clan kin not entrusting, yet took a different surname as heir; he violated ritual and drowned feeling, in order to confuse great human relations.”
translations.idiomatic: After Jia Chong’s death Qin Xiu argued, “He passed over his own kin to adopt an outsider as heir—sentiment trumping ritual and overturning the natural order.”

sentences.zh: 昔鄫養外孫莒公子為後，《春秋》書'莒人滅鄫'。

translations.literal: Formerly Zeng raised an outer grandson, the Prince of Ju’s son, as heir; the Spring and Autumn Annals wrote ‘Ju men extinguished Zeng.’
translations.idiomatic: When the state of Zeng made a grandson of Ju its heir, the *Spring and Autumn Annals* recorded that ‘the men of Ju destroyed Zeng.’”

sentences.zh: 聖人豈不知外孫親邪！

translations.literal: The sage surely knew outer grandsons are close!”
translations.idiomatic: The sage was hardly blind to affection for a daughter’s son!”

sentences.zh: 但以義推之，則無父子耳。

translations.literal: But by righteousness extrapolating it, then there is no father-son, that is all.”
translations.idiomatic: Measured by duty, that line severs the tie between father and son.”

sentences.zh: 又案詔書'自非功如太宰，始封無後如太宰，所取必己自出如太宰，不得以為比'。

translations.literal: Further examining the edict book: ‘Unless merit is like the Grand Preceptor’s, first enfeoffment without heir like the Grand Preceptor’s, what is taken must be self-issued like the Grand Preceptor’s—may not take this as comparison.’
translations.idiomatic: The edict itself says that unless merit equals the Grand Preceptor’s, unless a first enfeoffment truly lacks heirs, and unless the heir is still one’s own blood—as in the Grand Preceptor’s case—no precedent applies.”

sentences.zh: 然則以外孫為後，自非元功顯德，不之得也。

translations.literal: Then thus taking an outer grandson as heir, unless there is prime merit and illustrious virtue, it is not permissible.
translations.idiomatic: Adopting a daughter’s son is lawful only for founders of towering merit.”

sentences.zh: 天子之禮，蓋可然乎？

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven’s ritual—can it be so?”
translations.idiomatic: Can the rites of the Son of Heaven condone this?”

sentences.zh: 絕父祖之血食，開朝廷之禍門。

translations.literal: It cuts off father and grandfather’s blood sacrifice; it opens the court’s gate of disaster.
translations.idiomatic: It ends the sacrifices to his ancestors and opens the court to future usurpation.”

sentences.zh: 《諡法》'昏亂紀度曰荒'，請諡荒公。

translations.literal: The Posthumous-title Law: ‘Confusion and chaos of norms and measure is called huang’; request posthumously title Duke Huang.”
translations.idiomatic: The canon of posthumous names calls deliberate confusion of law ‘reckless’; let him be styled Duke of Recklessness.”

sentences.zh: 」不從。

translations.literal: ” They did not follow.
translations.idiomatic: The court refused.

sentences.zh: 王濬有平吳之勳，而為王渾所譖毀。

translations.literal: Wang Jun had the merit of pacifying Wu, yet was slandered and ruined by Wang Hun.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Jun had conquered Wu, yet Wang Hun slandered him.

sentences.zh: 帝雖不從，無明賞罰，以濬為輔國大將軍，天下咸為之怨。

translations.literal: The emperor although did not follow, had no clear reward and punishment; he made Jun General Who Aids the State; all under Heaven for it resented.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor took no clear stand: he named Wang Jun General Who Aids the State, a title the realm read as insult, not reward.

sentences.zh: 秀乃上言曰：「自大晉啟祚，輔國之號，率以舊恩。

translations.literal: Xiu thereupon submitted words, saying: “Since Great Jin opened the fortune, the title General Who Aids the State has generally been by old favor.”
translations.idiomatic: Qin Xiu therefore wrote, “Since our dynasty began, the title General Who Aids the State has gone to men honored for past favors, not for fresh merit.”

sentences.zh: 此為王濬無功之時，受九列之顯位，立功之後更得寵人之辱號也。

translations.literal: This is for Wang Jun at the time of lacking merit, receiving the nine ranks’ illustrious position; after establishing merit afterward again obtaining a favored person’s shameful title.”
translations.idiomatic: Wang Jun already held one of the nine top posts before he won any glory; to give him, after victory, the same empty title reserved for court favorites adds insult to his labors.”

sentences.zh: 四海視之，孰不失望！

translations.literal: The four seas look on it—who does not lose hope!
translations.idiomatic: The whole empire sees it—who would not feel betrayed?”

sentences.zh: 蜀小吳大，平蜀之後，二將皆就加三事，今濬還而降等，天下安得不惑乎！

translations.literal: Shu is small, Wu is large; after pacifying Shu, both generals alike received addition of the three offices; now Jun returns yet is lowered in rank—how can all under Heaven not be perplexed!
translations.idiomatic: Shu was the lesser foe and Wu the greater: after Shu fell, both generals who took part were raised to the three dukedoms, yet Wang Jun comes home from the greater conquest with a demotion—how can the realm not call that madness?”

sentences.zh: 吳之未亡也，雖以三祖之神武，猶躬受其屈。

translations.literal: When Wu had not yet perished, although by the three ancestors’ divine martialness, still personally they received its bending.
translations.idiomatic: While Wu still stood, even our dynasty’s three martial founders bowed to its strength in person.”

sentences.zh: 以孫皓之虛名，足以驚動諸夏，每一小出，雖聖心知其垂亡，然中國輒懷惶怖。

translations.literal: By Sun Hao’s empty name, it was enough to startle and move the various Xia; each time he made a small outing, although the sage heart knew it was about to perish, yet the central lands always harbored panic and fear.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Hao’s hollow prestige still shook the Central Plains: every minor sortie left the court, though convinced he was doomed, braced in dread.”

sentences.zh: 當爾時，有能借天子百萬之眾，平而有之，與國家結兄弟之交，臣恐朝野實皆甘之耳。

translations.literal: At that time, had there been one who could borrow the Son of Heaven’s million hosts, pacify and possess it, and with the state knot brotherhood’s relations, your subject fears court and countryside would in truth all have sweetly accepted it.
translations.idiomatic: Had anyone then been able to borrow the imperial armies, crush Wu, keep it, and treat the throne as an ally, I suspect every man in and out of court would have welcomed the bargain.”

sentences.zh: 今濬舉蜀、漢之卒，數旬而平吳，雖舉吳人之財寶以與之，本非己分有焉，而遽與計校乎？」

translations.literal: Now Jun raised Shu and Han’s soldiers, in several tens of days pacified Wu; even if one raised Wu people’s treasures and gave them to him, fundamentally it is not what in his allotment he had, yet hasten to reckon with him?”
translations.idiomatic: Wang Jun led the veterans of Shu and conquered Wu in weeks. You could heap on him every treasure Wu owned—none of it would be more than his due—yet you haggle over his reward?”

sentences.zh: 後與劉暾等同議齊王攸事，忤旨，除名。

translations.literal: Later together with Liu Tun and others he deliberated on Prince of Qi You’s affair, offended intent, was stripped of name.
translations.idiomatic: Later he joined Liu Tun and others in debating Prince Sima You’s case, crossed the emperor, and was dismissed from the rolls.

sentences.zh: 尋復起為博士。

translations.literal: Before long he was again raised to be erudit.
translations.idiomatic: Soon he was recalled as an erudit.

sentences.zh: 秀性悻直，與物多忤。

translations.literal: Xiu’s nature was resentful and straight; with things he often opposed.
translations.idiomatic: Qin Xiu was blunt and uncompromising and often collided with the world.

sentences.zh: 為博士前後垂二十年，卒於官。

translations.literal: As erudit before and after nearly twenty years, he died in office.
translations.idiomatic: He spent almost twenty years as an erudit and died in that post.

sentences.zh: 【史評】

translations.literal: Historians’ appraisal.
translations.idiomatic: Historians’ commentary

sentences.zh: 史臣曰：齊獻王以明德茂親，經邦論道，允厘庶績，式敘彝倫。

translations.literal: The historiographer-ministers say: Prince Xian of Qi, by enlightened virtue and luxuriant kinship, regulated the state and discussed the Way, truly ordered the many accomplishments, patterned and ordered constant human relations.
translations.idiomatic: The historians write: Prince Sima You of Qi, a kinsman of shining virtue, set policy for the realm, brought order to every branch of government, and gave shape to moral relations.

sentences.zh: 武帝納奸諂之邪謀，懷紹終之遠慮，遂乃君茲青土，作牧東籓。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu accepted treacherous flattery’s evil stratagem, harbored continuing-the-line’s distant planning; thereupon he lorded this green earth, became shepherd of the eastern feudatory.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wu listened to sycophants, brooded on securing his line, and sent that prince to rule the green fields of Qi as shepherd of the eastern marches.

sentences.zh: 遠邇驚嗟，朝野失望。

translations.literal: Far and near were startled and sighed; court and countryside lost hope.
translations.idiomatic: Near and far were stunned; court and country alike despaired.

sentences.zh: 曹志等服膺教義，方軌儒門，蹇蹇匪躬，慺慺體國。

translations.literal: Cao Zhi and others wore on the breast teaching’s meaning, squared tracks with the Confucian gate, stubbornly not self, anxiously embodied the state.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Zhi and his fellows took Confucian teaching to heart, walked the scholar’s path, risked themselves without flinching, and burned for the dynasty’s good.

sentences.zh: 故能抗言鳳闕，忤犯龍鱗，身雖暫屈，道亦弘矣！

translations.literal: Therefore they were able to oppose speech at the phoenix tower, offend and violate dragon scales; although the body for a time bent, the Way also was great!
translations.idiomatic: So they could speak truth in the phoenix halls and stroke the dragon the wrong way: though their careers suffered for it, the Way they served grew only greater.”

sentences.zh: 庾氏世載清德，見稱於世，汝潁之多奇士，斯焉取斯。

translations.literal: The Yu clan generation carried pure virtue, was praised in the generation; Run and Ying’s many strange knights—this is where they took this from.
translations.idiomatic: The Yu house bred generation on generation of unstained honor and produced the sort of rare talent the Run-Ying country was famous for.”

sentences.zh: 謀甫素疾佞邪，而發因醉飽，投鼠忌器，豈易由言。

translations.literal: Moufu always hated flattery and evil, yet outbreak was because of drunk satiety; casting a rat, fearing the vessel—how is it easy to proceed by words.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Chun always despised sycophants but burst out in his cups—one fears to strike the rat beside the priceless vase, and frank speech is never easy.”

sentences.zh: 竊人之財，猶謂之盜，子玄假譽攘善，將非盜乎！

translations.literal: Stealing people’s wealth, still is called banditry; Zixuan borrowed fame and seized the good—will it not be banditry!
translations.idiomatic: To steal another’s goods is theft: Guo Xiang stole another’s reputation—is that not theft as well?”

sentences.zh: 贊曰：魏氏維城，濟北知名。

translations.literal: The encomium says: Wei’s bulwark city—north of the Ji, his name was known.
translations.idiomatic: Encomium: As bulwark of the house of Wei, the Prince of Jibei won lasting fame.

sentences.zh: 潁川多士，峻亦飛英。

translations.literal: Yingchuan had many knights; Jun also flew in excellence.
translations.idiomatic: Yingchuan bred many great men, and Yu Jun rose among them.

sentences.zh: 長岑徇義，祭酒遺榮。

translations.literal: Changcen followed righteousness; the libationer left glory behind.
translations.idiomatic: The Baron of Changcen died for loyalty; the Libationer turned his back on empty glory.

sentences.zh: 謀甫三爵，酗醟斯作。

translations.literal: Moufu three goblets; drunken brew then was made.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Moufu’s third cup loosed the drunken brawl.

sentences.zh: 象既攘善，秀惟癉惡。

translations.literal: Xiang having seized the good, Xiu only hated evil.
translations.idiomatic: Guo Xiang stole credit; Qin Xiu lashed out at vice.

sentences.zh: 旉獻嘉謀，幾趨鼎鑊。

translations.literal: Bin presented fine stratagems, almost hastened to cauldron and axe.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Bin offered wise counsel and nearly landed in the execution pot.
